item.title: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together
item.abstract: Back to Articles Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together Enterprise Article Published November 9, 2026 Upvote 4 Alex M Tseng alexmtseng Follow amazon Higher-Order Pruning of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models Introduction Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used. Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization . Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove. Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance . Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates. Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method. In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers . item.title: Meta releases Muse Ember, a new lightweight model for agent execution
item.abstract: Meta Superintelligence Lab released a new AI model on Monday called Muse Ember, the lab’s lightest and most cost-efficient AI model yet. In its release, Meta said Ember was “designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.” Meta particularly emphasized Ember’s cost-per-task, using Artificial Analysis’s composite benchmark score to show Ember as cheaper and smarter than competitors like Anthropic’s Haiku and OpenAI’s Luna. Image Credits: Meta Superintelligence Labs At 10 cents per million input tokens, Ember is significantly cheaper than frontier competitors like Haiku and Luna. Not only that, it’s cost-competitive with open source competitors like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 Flash. Given the emphasis on low cost and accuracy at scale, Ember is designed to pair with a larger model like Meta’s Muse Wonder in an agentic harness. In the case of a customer-support agent, for instance, you might see a heavier model establishing rules for how to handle a particular issue, then sending a lighter-weight model to apply the rules across tens of thousands of cases. As Meta puts it in the announcement, “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.” With volume-heavy use cases in mind, Meta also trained Ember to work well across different types of media, including text, images, and audio. The result makes the model surprisingly flexible in what kind of inputs it can handle. As Meta puts it in the announcement, “agents can read screenshots, charts, and scanned documents, or work from voice memos, meeting recordings, and video without a separate model.” Ember is the fourth model released under Meta’s Muse brand, following the mid-weight Spark ( released in April ), Spark’s open source twin Glimmer ( released in August ), and the Wonder frontier model ( released in October ). The flagship consumer AI product, the Muse Agent, was released in September to unexpected success , with new features like Spaces and video chat rolling out earlier this month.

item.title: 0sec Labs Open-Sources 0, an AI Security Harness With Web UI, CLI and MCP
item.abstract: Zurich-based 0sec Labs has released 0 , an open-source AI security harness. It runs vulnerability investigations, code review, pentesting, reverse engineering and fix generation. Developers drive it from a local browser console, a headless CLI or an MCP server . The 0sec Labs open-source AI security harness is licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0 and ships as a research preview. 0 is a control plane around LLMs and security tools. It is not a model. You plug in a provider, and 0 runs scoped workflows against authorized targets. The research team describes it as a self-evolving, multi-model harness . 0sec Labs is backed by Y Combinator . The architecture docs state one rule: reproduce before trusting. Agentic scans follow a conceptual pipeline: Web pentesting is shell-first. The agent uses bash with curl, python3 and sqlmap, not a fixed HTTP tool set. Evidence carries a proof grade from candidate to impact-proven . Compiled targets go through 0verse , a separate in-repo engine. It wraps Ghidra, angr and AFL++. Its local MCP server exposes 9 tools for scanning, triage, PoVs and reports. Installation is one script. Running 0 opens the local browser console without an account. The console has chat, a findings queue and board, workflow templates, skills and memory. Coding agents connect through 0 mcp-server --workflows . The CLI exposes the same workflow runner with commands like 0 workflow run and 0 runs list . Model access is bring-your-own. The API keys page lists OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, Azure, Qwen, Kimi, GLM and Grok. It also supports Claude, Codex and Gemini CLI runtimes. All scores below are self-reported. The recorded cost was about $5.20 per solved XBOW challenge . The research page lists 30+ merged Linux kernel 0-days. Disclosures span Bluetooth, NFC, mac802154, TIPC and mlx5e subsystems. Library CVEs include jsonata, node-forge, protobuf.js and Wireshark. The open-source harness is free. You pay your model provider. A hosted version, 0cloud , is on a waitlist. The pricing page lists $100 in trial credits and $5 per PR security test. Check out the GitHub repo , docs and research disclosures . item.title: Pluggable Agentic AI Framework: A seven-layer composable enterprise agentic AI reference architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.abstract: “How do we run our AI agents in production at scale?” is the question every customer eventually asks. It comes bundled with several questions. How do we handle thousands of concurrent user requests securely and confidently? How do we make sure the agents stay reliable under real traffic instead of failing silently? How do we know if an agent still meets the quality and safety standards it passed during testing? What are agent security best practices? Should that be deterministic or non-deterministic? And many more. A proof-of-concept answers none of these, because it is built to show the agent model can do the task, not to survive production traffic, cost pressure, and security review. That gap between a working prototype and a system that runs reliably, securely, frugally and responsibly at scale, is where most agentic AI initiatives stall, and it is rarely the model’s fault. Every team building an agent tends to rebuild the same scaffolding from scratch: its own routing logic, its own guardrails, its own observability, all applied after the fact rather than built in from the start. The teams need a shared, production-ready architecture that every agent can build on. This post walks through a seven-layer composable reference architecture designed to take multi-agent AI applications from prototype to production scale. The Pluggable Agentic AI Framework is a reference architecture for multi-agent applications organized into seven layers , each with a distinct responsibility and a stable contract. The services and technologies shown in each layer reflect the reference implementation, not mandatory choices. Organizations can substitute alternatives that align with their existing infrastructure and requirements. Together, these layers offer a blueprint for building, securing, and operating agentic AI applications at production scale. Figure 1: The seven layers of the Pluggable Agentic AI Framework Data and Knowledge is the foundation of Agentic AI. An agent is only as good as the data it can access. Whether an agent is checking out a healthcare formulary, tracking inventory, or interpreting a compliance rule, it needs relevant, up-to-date information to answer correctly. This layer owns retrieval, embeddings, and access to structured and unstructured data through a clear contract and protocol: accept a query and return the most relevant information that acts as context for an agent. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base , Vector Engine for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless , Amazon S3 Vectors and Amazon DynamoDB are example building blocks for this foundation. Model and Inference choices should be driven by configuration, not hardwired into agent or application logic. Use smaller, faster models for simple tasks and larger models for requests that require more nuanced reasoning. It is important to conduct a thorough model evaluation for the use case you are building with realistic and representative business data. A model routing layer keeps AI agents decoupled from the model hosting environment and provider-specific APIs by relying on a consistent request-and-response contract. A proxy such as LiteLLM provides a common interface across providers, so you can switch models based on your evaluations without rewriting application logic. Orchestration determines how work is distributed, and choosing the right approach is critical. For straightforward tasks, use a single agent to handle the work from end to end. For complex, cross-domain workflows, use a supervisor to delegate specialist agents, each scoped to a specific capability and tied to a specific set of tools. Avoid building one agent that does everything. As tools, instructions, and context accumulate, the context window grows, latency increases, and accuracy can suffer. Tool sprawl sets in, which can push agents beyond their intended boundaries, leading to unintended actions and security breaches. Splitting responsibilities keeps each agent’s context focused and makes latency more predictable. You can also test each agent’s behavior, scale it, and define its security model independently. Enforce bounded autonomy: specialists should execute strictly within the tools they have been granted, and nothing more. In addition to decomposing into specific specialists and setting its boundary, decouple the specialist agents from the supervisor agents. Allow the supervisor to discover the specialists from a centralized agent registry and invoke them through a standardized protocol like MCP (Model Context Protocol) and A2A (Agent to Agent). Maintain a centralized agent registry that catalogs every agent’s tools, skills, and owner. This gives your organization the visibility it needs for governance at scale, increases the velocity of AI agent implementation through reusability, and avoids the cost of repetitive development. Consider using Strands Agents for specialists, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness for the orchestrator, AWS Agent Registry and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway for centralized discovery and routing. Security and Guardrails should be a primary concern, built into the design from day one. Agentic AI exposes organizations to a new class of risks that conventional security frameworks were not built to address, from prompt injection and tool misuse to memory and data poisoning. Treat all external content as untrusted by default. Authenticate every request, whether it comes from a user, another agent, or an automated workflow, through a service like Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity . Then use fine-grained access control to determine whether each tool call is permitted before execution. Grant agents temporary, scoped credentials instead of persistent secrets. On the data-protection side, mask sensitive data like PHI (Personal Health Information) and PII (Personally Identifiable Information) in agent and tool requests and responses, so that sensitive customer information does not appear in agent outputs or lingers in memory. For accountability, capture every significant decision in a tamper-evident audit trail, route high-impact actions through a human approval gate, and deploy circuit breakers to halt anomalous behavior before it can escalate. Consider using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for user inputs, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity and Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for authentication and access control, along with AWS Security and governance controls to bring defense-in-depth security. Application is where the end-user experience lives, whether that is a chat interface, an API surface, or an embedded widget. Keep this layer intentionally thin. Its only responsibilities should be presenting the conversation and passing requests to the orchestration layer beneath it. Resist the urge to embed business logic here. The cleaner the separation, the more easily you can iterate on the user experience without destabilizing the backend. A decision model can sit at this boundary as a fast, inexpensive check: in one call it scores whether a request is in scope, needs a human, or is urgent, returning probabilities instead of free text. Your code acts on those scores with simple thresholds, answering off-topic requests directly and flagging escalations, so the full agentic loop runs only when it adds value. When building the application layer, think about what would be needed for another AI agent to consume and interact with your AI agents along with humans. Build your external interfaces accordingly. Observability should watch every layer from day one, not after the first incident. Along with the logs and metrics, end-to-end agent traces are critical to measure whether the agent performed its task correctly. Along with the trace, collect cost and token usage per request, time to first token, whether the call is secure, and surface dashboards for latency, error rates, and spend before you go live. Proactive monitoring is cheaper than reactive firefighting.

item.title: Reason Machines Open-Sources Aspen, a Git Server Built for AI Agents
item.abstract: Reason Machines has released Aspen , an open-source Git server for AI agent traffic. It targets repositories that hundreds of agents push to at once. Aspen independently implements the design OpenAI described for Pando. Aspen is a self-hostable Git server from Reason Machines that scales writes per branch, not per repository. It speaks plain Git over HTTPS and SSH. Packs go to S3-compatible object storage; branch history goes to PostgreSQL. An agent pushes every few minutes, and CI fetches after each push. Per Reason Machines , a classic server queues every push to a repository together. It also builds a fresh pack for every fetch. Server work grows with clients, not with new code. OpenAI hit this wall and built Pando. It cut median push latency by nearly 5x and serves nearly a petabyte daily. Aspen follows Pando and drops 2 claims most Git servers keep. Each branch is a chain of versions in one Postgres row. A push uploads its pack, then moves the branch with one compare-and-swap. Pushes to different branches never wait for each other. If 2 pushes race on one branch, one wins. The other gets Git’s usual “fetch first” error. The cost: branches may be read at slightly different moments. Aspen never unpacks a push. It checks the pack, completes missing bases and stores it as-is. A fetch streams stored packs the client lacks, recompressing nothing. Signed URLs can serve packs from a CDN. A push sees only the trunk branch, so negotiation stays small with a million branches. Background compaction merges packs 16 at a time, in levels like a log-structured merge tree. A client far behind gets a few dozen packs, not thousands. Depth-1 CI fetches get a tip pack built once and served to every job. The test used one 8-core server, S3 Standard and a 4-core Postgres. The target was a copy of git.git, about 4,500 files and 75,000 commits. Aspen sustained 567 pushes per second for 5 minutes with no errors. Each push reached S3 and Postgres before Git printed “ok.” Cursor reports up to 120 pushes per second for Origin on S3 Standard. On S3 Express One Zone it exceeds 300. That is a replicated cluster on Cursor’s monorepo, so setups differ. The README calls Aspen’s figures indicative, not performance claims. You build from source with Rust. aspen dev runs everything with SQLite and a local directory. Teams get Docker Compose with PostgreSQL and MinIO, plus a Helm chart. Terraform covers AWS, Google Cloud, Azure and Hetzner. Mirror mode fronts GitHub or GitLab, so you can trial it without migrating. The live demo is a 64 x 64 pixel canvas where each click is one pushed commit. Per the company, one Reason agent built Aspen from first commit to public in 4 days. That took 151 merged PRs. item.title: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 on AWS
item.abstract: Today, we are announcing the availability of Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS. Claude Fable 5.2 is Anthropic’s most capable generally available model for technical work that raises the bar in coding and the sciences. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available through Anthropic’s verification programs for advanced work in cyber security and life sciences. In this post, we cover what’s new in both models, why Fable 5.2 matters for your technical workloads, and how to get started building with the model on Amazon Bedrock. Fable 5.2 raises the bar on the hardest problems in coding, math, and science. It takes on ambiguous, multi-step work, verifies its own output, and can run unattended for hours to days. It interprets prompts, iterates, catches its own errors, and optimizes as it goes. In Anthropic’s alignment testing, Mythos 5.2 hallucinates less, completes tasks more reliably, surfaces important information more consistently, and self-reports issues more honestly than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1. Anthropic expects Fable 5.2 to behave similarly. If a cyber security query is declined, you can retry it on Opus 4.8, and if a biology query is declined, you can retry it on Opus 5. On Amazon Bedrock, the retry is your code’s job, not an automatic switch. If the declined request hit the prompt cache, the refusal also includes a fallback credit token. Send that token with the retry and it’s billed as cache reads, so you don’t pay to write the same cache twice. Check the documentation for more information on fallback credit. For authorized work in cyber security and life sciences, Claude Mythos 5.2 is available through Anthropic’s verification programs . Mythos 5.2 covers two high-risk domains, available only through the verification programs noted earlier: Anthropic designates Claude Fable 5.2 as a Covered Model . By default, its use requires retention for up to 30 days and human safety review. On Amazon Bedrock, Amazon personnel perform the review within the AWS boundary. Set the aws_review data retention mode on your account or project before you invoke the model. See Amazon Bedrock data retention for more details. Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS), built in collaboration with AWS, combines the privacy of zero data retention (ZDR) with the latest safeguards for detecting misuse. EFS is available now. A version that keeps your data in a bucket and under keys you control is expected to follow, and it has not launched yet. Until it does, eligible customers can use Fable 5.2 with zero data retention through June 30, 2027. To try Fable 5.2, open the Amazon Bedrock console , choose Test , Playground , and select Fable 5.2 as the model. From there, you can run a prompt directly against it. Programmatically, you can call the model with the Anthropic Messages API against bedrock-runtime (through the Anthropic SDK). You can also stay on the Invoke and Converse APIs on bedrock-runtime through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and AWS SDK . To follow along with the code examples in this post, you need the following: Here’s a quick example using the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3): You can explore the Getting Started notebook for more examples. For teams already running Claude models on Amazon Bedrock, the claude-api skill in Claude Code helps you upgrade to Fable 5.2. The claude-api skill is an open-source skill built into Claude Code that captures the details that make Claude API code work well. It covers which agent patterns fit a given job, what parameters change between model generations, and when to apply prompt caching. It stays current as Anthropic’s SDKs evolve: when a new model is released or the API gains a feature, the skill already knows. When you ask Claude Code to upgrade your codebase to Fable 5.2, the skill reviews your code and walks you through: The skill also detects your deployment platform including Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, and other environments and adjusts model ID formats and feature configurations accordingly. For example, it uses the Amazon Bedrock structured model ID format ( global.anthropic.claude-fable-5-2 ). In Claude Code, run the migration directly: This scans your working directory (or a subdirectory or specific file list you confirm) and applies the migration changes in a single guided pass. You can also invoke it conversationally by telling Claude Code: The claude-api skill is available in Claude Code and is also bundled into CodeRabbit, JetBrains IDEs (including Junie), Resolve AI, and Warp. It is open source at anthropics/skills on GitHub, so any coding agent can integrate it. Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are available today on Amazon Bedrock through US Geo CRIS and Global CRIS inference profiles. See the Bedrock documentation for the full list of supported Regions. For pricing information, see Amazon Bedrock pricing . Both models are also available through Claude Platform on AWS in every Region where the service is offered. Give Claude Fable 5.2 a try in the Amazon Bedrock console , in Claude Platform on AWS , or explore the Getting Started notebook on GitHub.

item.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
item.abstract: Today, we’re announcing that NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. You can deploy it with a few steps in SageMaker Studio or with a few lines of the SageMaker Python SDK. Super VL is the vision-language model (VLM) in the NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 family. It accepts images, video, and text as input and generates text. The model pairs a 120B-parameter hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language backbone with 12B active parameters and a C-RADIO vision encoder. It supports context lengths of up to 1 million tokens and includes a built-in Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head that supports speculative decoding. You can configure reasoning per request. NVIDIA built Super VL for document intelligence, GUI understanding for computer-use agents, video question answering, and multimodal agentic applications. JumpStart offers two variants: NVFP4, quantized from BF16 with quantization-aware distillation for optimized inference, and the BF16 full-precision reference weights. In this post, we walk through the model’s capabilities and the JumpStart deployment configurations. We then show the measured inference performance and demonstrate text, image, and video inference. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120B-parameter model with 12B active parameters per token. It combines a hybrid language backbone with a dedicated vision encoder. The following table compares the specifications of the two variants available in JumpStart. Super VL is aimed at agentic workloads that must see and read. It targets vision-language agents that combine reasoning, coding, tool use, document understanding, and video understanding. The NVIDIA model cards report results for both checkpoints across reasoning, coding, agentic, long-context, and multimodal benchmarks, with evaluation settings held constant so that only the checkpoint differs. The following table highlights the multimodal benchmarks most relevant to vision-language workloads (reasoning on). NVFP4, the JumpStart default, matches BF16 on MMLongBench-Doc and stays within about one point on the others, scoring slightly higher on OCRBench v2 and OSWorld-Verified. For the full comparison against other publicly available models and the evaluation settings, see the NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Lightning Technical Report . We measured inference performance with the JumpStart release container using the generate workload profile: 250 input tokens, 1,500 output tokens, and five concurrent streaming requests. Throughput is the mean output tokens per second for each request, and time to first token is the mean across requests. These results illustrate the deployment choices available through JumpStart. The NVFP4 variant runs on G7 instances with a smaller GPU footprint. The BF16 variant on ml.p5en.48xlarge achieved 140.85 output tokens per second per request in this test. Time to first token remained about half a second across all three configurations. Because the variants run on different GPU systems and configurations, these measurements are not an isolated BF16-versus-NVFP4 precision comparison. Longer prompts change the picture: with the summarize profile (10,000 input tokens), time to first token on ml.g7.24xlarge is 12.62 seconds. SageMaker JumpStart supports Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on the following validated instance types. NVFP4 runs on G7 instances with NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, and BF16 runs on P5en instances with NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The JumpStart default instance for NVFP4 is ml.g7.24xlarge, which serves as the recommended starting point for the generate profile. The checkpoint includes the MTP head, but the JumpStart serving configuration does not enable speculative decoding. You can deploy the model from SageMaker Studio, with the SageMaker Python SDK, or from the Hugging Face model page. Before you deploy, make sure you have the following: To deploy the model from SageMaker Studio, complete the following steps: Figure 1: Searching for NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL in SageMaker JumpStart Figure 2: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL NVFP4 model card in SageMaker JumpStart Choose BF16 if you need the full-precision reference weights on ml.p5en.48xlarge. The following screenshot shows the BF16 model card. Figure 3: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL BF16 model card in SageMaker JumpStart Figure 4: Reviewing Nemotron 3.5 Super VL capabilities and model details before deployment Figure 5: SageMaker endpoint deployment in progress before the status reaches InService The example uses the SageMaker Python SDK v3 classes: JumpStartConfig names the model, ModelBuilder builds and deploys it, and deploy returns an Endpoint resource. Pass the instance type in Compute , because the SDK falls back to ml.m5.large when the instance type is absent, and the build then fails. The deploy call waits until the endpoint is InService, which takes about 10 minutes on ml.g7.24xlarge. The inference_config_name argument selects a serving configuration, and each configuration sets a different context length. The default generate configurations serve a 2,275-token context sized for short prompts. The summarize configurations serve 13,650 tokens, and the modify configurations serve 15,600 tokens. The example uses a modify configuration because the inference examples in this post, especially image, video, and reasoning requests, need the larger context. All the inference examples that follow assume the modify configuration. You can also deploy the model from its Hugging Face model page: choose Deploy , then Amazon SageMaker AI , and continue to the SageMaker deployment workflow. Figure 6: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model page on Hugging Face with the Deploy menu On the deployment menu, choose Amazon SageMaker AI to open the SageMaker deployment workflow, as shown in the following screenshot. Figure 7: Selecting Amazon SageMaker AI from the Hugging Face deployment workflow After the endpoint is InService, you can send inference requests to it. The JumpStart endpoint exposes a vLLM-powered chat completions API, so applications can send inference requests using a familiar chat-message format. NVIDIA recommends temperature 1.0 and top_p 0.95 for text, and temperature 0.6 and top_p 0.95 for image and video requests. You must send media inline as base64 data URLs because the endpoint runs with network isolation and cannot fetch URLs. Reasoning is on by default, and you can configure it per request. The reasoning text is returned in the reasoning field of the message, separate from content. For direct extraction-style tasks, you can disable reasoning with enable_thinking=False in chat_template_kwargs . The model accepts images rather than raw PDF files. To process a PDF, render each page to an image such as PNG before sending it to the model. A 1,536 x 1,024 page costs about 1,536 tokens of context, and one request can carry one image. The following example sends a short MP4 clip as a base64-encoded data URL and asks the model to summarize it, with reasoning disabled for a direct response. For video inference, use short, compressed clips and keep the encoded request within the endpoint’s supported payload limits. For reasoning-intensive video requests, set max_tokens high enough to allow the model to complete its reasoning while considering response length and endpoint invocation limits. Consider the following recommendations when you run Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on SageMaker JumpStart: To avoid ongoing charges, delete the endpoint, the endpoint configuration, and the model when you are done: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL brings image, video, and document understanding to SageMaker JumpStart. The NVFP4 variant is available on G7 instances with NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. The BF16 variant is available on ml.p5en.48xlarge with NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Choose NVFP4 for optimized inference with model quality close to the BF16 checkpoint, or BF16 when you want the full-precision reference weights.

item.title: Anthropic releases new Mythos and Fable models amid RSI concerns
item.abstract: Anthropic released new versions of its most advanced models on Monday, with the launch of Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2. The company says the new models “show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision” and communicate more clearly with users. Notably, Anthropic is lowering the cost of Fable from $10 to $8 per million input tokens. As a result, Fable 5.2 is now cheaper than its primary competitor GPT-6 Astra. Anthropic says that the new version of Fable will return responses 30% faster across effort levels. Faster inference serving is available for double the price. Fable 5.2 is also compatible with zero data retention (ZDR) policies through the Enterprise Frontier Safeguards system , long a sticking point for many enterprise clients. It’s Anthropic’s first model release since the arrival of a third-party report from the assessment group METR , which suggested the lab might be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) — or the ability for AI models to carry on model training independently. The METR report found internal models were speeding up Anthropic’s AI progress by roughly 2x, although many uncertainties remain. Still, Anthropic’s release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. “Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow.” Anthropic maintains that the new version of Mythos does not have the ability to act covertly against its user, a verdict that’s detailed further in Mythos 5.2’s system card . “Claude Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities than prior Claude models on several of our evaluations, particularly when its reasoning is hidden from the monitor,” the system card reads. “That said, we believe that low levels of absolute performance on our new covert evaluations support claims that rely on detection of harmful actions in high-stakes situations.” Fable 5.2 has been available to select parties in pre-release for some time, and Anthropic says the model has already “solved two open problems in theoretical physics, formalized Fermat’s Last Theorem, and supported numerous other research projects.” Also on Monday, AI startup Physical Superintelligence announced a new proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture, a pivotal step in setting theoretical limits for quantum computing. Notably, the lab said the result was achieved by running “a non-public Anthropic model” within PSI’s own system. Anthropic did not confirm or deny whether Fable 5.2 was the model in question.

item.title: TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max
item.abstract:
Our newest TPUs: 8tx and 8i Max, built for the agentic era Nov 09, 2026 | We’ve expanded our eighth generation TPU portfolio with TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, marking four new TPU systems in a single year. Amin Vahdat SVP and Chief Technologist, AI and Infrastructure Read AI-generated summary We’re expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with the new TPU 8tx for secure, confidential inference and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows. These systems help you manage complex agentic workloads by providing specialized hardware for security, density, and reasoning. You can learn more about these additions and our latest software updates by watching our broadcast or visiting the Google Cloud website to explore our full infrastructure lineup. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with the new TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max systems. TPU 8tx provides hardware-level security for sensitive data, while TPU 8i Max handles massive context windows. These systems join TPU 8t and TPU 8i to offer specialized performance for every AI lifecycle stage. We are making TPUs more accessible by supporting PyTorch, open-source software, and automated tools for developers. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points We first designed TPUs more than a decade ago motivated by Google’s internal demands, including voice recognition and language translation. Eight generations of TPUs later, the use cases have exploded, covering: i) training and serving our own Gemini models, ii) agentic workloads, iii) delivering services to Google Cloud customers on our cloud infrastructure, and most recently, iv) allowing customers to deploy TPUs directly into their own data centers. TPUs are now a rapidly growing business with nearly 100 customers — including frontier labs, trading firms, retailers, universities, and more. At Google Cloud Next in April, we introduced two new specialized TPUs in the same generation — 8t for large-scale training and 8i for real-time reasoning. TPU 8t and 8i offer up to 2.7 times better training performance and 80% better inference price performance, respectively, versus our previous generation of TPUs. Today, we’re taking that a step further, expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with two additional systems: TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack, and TPU 8tx for secure and confidential inference. This is the first time we have introduced four TPU systems in a single year. Our expanded eighth-generation TPU portfolio: TPU 8t, TPU 8i, TPU 8tx, and TPU 8i Max. While we’ve always co-designed our TPUs in partnership with Google DeepMind, we’re now increasingly getting feedback from external organizations on their specific needs. With computing moving from human to agent scale, businesses are asking for accelerators that can reason across AI models’ massive context windows. In addition, some highly regulated customers are asking for specialized encryption capabilities for unique workloads. The new TPU systems we are announcing today address this new reality. Coupled with our recent PyTorch announcements , our aim is to make TPUs more easily accessible to every developer and Cloud customer. By combining modular custom silicon with an open and easy-to-use software stack, we can deliver new hardware and system configurations at the pace of the AI industry. Building the computer around the chip Today, we’re announcing two new TPU systems — and there’s an important difference between a new chip and a new system. Designing a new chip means laying out billions of microscopic transistors on a silicon wafer in a multi-year process bound by the laws of physics and a complex, long-duration manufacturing lifecycle. A system, on the other hand, is about how we bring together the compute, networking, and storage around the chip. This can include how they are packaged with the chips, to quickly meet emerging customer needs and research use cases. When we built our very first TPU more than a decade ago, we knew AI software would evolve much faster than silicon manufacturing ever could. So we made a foundational bet on system balance and modularity, architecting our TPUs as building blocks as part of our AI Hypercomputer , so engineers could rapidly adjust packaging, high-speed memory, optical networking, and security around them. That approach allows us to deliver specialized supercomputers in a matter of months rather than years. Specializing for secure, high-context AI Each system in our eighth-generation TPU portfolio targets a distinct part of the AI lifecycle. TPU 8t and TPU 8i established the baseline for this generation of chips: TPU 8t was designed to be a training powerhouse for massive foundation models with maximum “goodput” — or the useful intelligence delivered per watt of energy used. TPU 8i is the reasoning engine, designed to break the memory wall, cutting inter-chip communication delays by up to half. Now, as enterprises bring autonomous agents into production, we have created two new configurations of these foundational systems to solve two urgent new challenges: hardware-level data security and million-token context scale. TPU 8tx TPU 8tx, our third eighth-generation system, is optimized for secure and confidential inference and is also great for small-scale training. It’s built for regulated enterprises and governments running frontier or proprietary models and autonomous agents alongside their most sensitive data. Normally, data is encrypted when stored or sent over a network, but has to be unlocked in memory while a computer processes it. Built on the same silicon as TPU 8t and paired with 5th Generation AMD EPYC CPU hosts, TPU 8tx builds security directly into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use. And by adopting the same low-latency Boardfly network we created for real-time reasoning, TPU 8tx keeps multi-step agents moving, delivering up to 2x lower latency compared to TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty. Pairing training-grade compute with a fast inference network also means organizations can simultaneously run and customize their models on a single system. TPU 8tx enables teams to fine-tune models using their private data, distill large models into smaller ones, and train their agents through reinforcement learning, all without needing to migrate sensitive data between separate clusters. Designed for sensitive enterprise workloads, TPU 8tx provides hardware-level confidential compute for private fine-tuning and secure agent execution. TPU 8i Max Our fourth system, TPU 8i Max, is built for a different problem: the memory wall. When dozens of AI agents work together across an entire software codebase or hours of video at once, memory bandwidth quickly becomes the bottleneck. So we took two low-latency TPU 8i chips and combined them onto a single package. TPU 8i Max scales compute and memory in lockstep, delivering double the compute, double the SRAM and double the HBM bandwidth of TPU 8i, so processors remain equipped with essential data and so that large workloads do not stall. Further, because TPU 8i Max fits twice the silicon within the existing rack footprint, data centers can deploy significantly more computing power per square foot and per watt. The dual-chip TPU 8i Max system, engineered for massive context windows and maximum compute density. While flexible across workloads, together the four systems in our eighth-generation TPUs give customers a purpose-built accelerator for every stage of the agentic lifecycle. TPU 8t for scale-up training, TPU 8i for low-latency reasoning, TPU 8tx for confidential computing, and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack.

item.title: AI R&D Is Accelerating Towards Potential RSI in 2027
item.abstract: METR came out with an extensive report on how much AI is accelerating AI R&D at Anthropic, and thus how close we might be to recursive self-improvement (RSI) and how far that might go. This is one of the most important questions in the world. Their answer: Things are already accelerating on the order of a 2x speedup. This is several months ahead of the AI 2027 timeline. A naive extrapolation says we may be less than a year away from full RSI. There are no clear bottlenecks in the way. This report updated many towards shorter timelines. This is consistent with what OpenAI and Anthropic themselves have been saying, and with extrapolation from the progress we are observing. We are running out of time. That doesn’t have to be the way this plays out. We could stop the labs. The labs could choose to stop. Or the estimates could be wrong, or some bottlenecks could be hit, or the results could be less impactful than we expect. Indeed do many things come to pass. And if it does happen this quickly, one would expect it to go quite poorly, and likely to cause everyone to die, but perhaps it goes well. METR : These conclusions are based on key empirical findings from the full report. Some of the key findings that most informed our conclusions about risk were redacted. ​ Ajeya Cotra (METR): For the last few months, some of my colleagues at METR have been working on a deep-access investigation to understand how much Anthropic is being accelerated by its AI systems. From my reading of their report and Anthropic’s RSP, it looks like the “dramatic acceleration” threshold has already been crossed. I do not find either of these results surprising. I made minor updates towards faster outcomes and fewer bottlenecks, but not major ones. I had already made major ones. The situation looks rather grim. But this is not a surprise. The information from inside the labs makes you think the situation is grim and timelines are short, but those with that information were already shouting from the rooftops that their secret information meant the situation is grim and timelines were short. Why did you not think this was the standard reaction to their information? I did find it surprising that so many found this surprising, including METR. Their team did not expect substantial acceleration. Ryan Greenblatt expected only 1.15x-1.3x speedup this year . Six weeks ago in the Opus 5.5 system card the estimate was at least a 1.5x speedup . If you are making major updates in response to this report, that is probably good and wise, but indicates you had previously made a mistake in your estimations. If you only look at public models, you can make a case that there is a step change at Mythos but that otherwise the rate of progress has not changed. I was always skeptical of that, but it was a valid claim. Add in the orange data points from internal models and you cannot tell that story. When we include the recent additional internal releases, this takes the estimate from the ~1.7x in the Haiku system card up to a new estimate of ~1.9x. Peter Wildeford : It seems important to realize that: – AI companies have unreleased internal models that are more powerful than the public ones we plebs have access to – Only when you account for these internal models, you can see that AI progress is actually accelerating faster than before – AI companies use their AIs with like 10,000x more compute than us plebs, so they can do much more than we can even with the same AIs You could also have gotten to a similar result by extrapolating the automation graph: Benjamin Todd : Extrapolating Anthropic’s internal AI R&D data results in Claude leading internal research by mid-2027, and plausibly near full automation by the end of 2027, lining up with other methods. (h/t @luc_feron ) The information METR is relying on most is largely redacted. The public report centers on AECI and other estimates. METR is implying that such arguments are merely the legible case they are allowed to make, and that there is a stronger case. Kudos to Anthropic for allowing this investigation. METR : Anthropic offered unprecedented access to internal data on their AI R&D process, including a variety of metrics on pretraining, reinforcement learning (RL), training compute in each domain, benchmark scores for internal models, AI speedup analyses, forecasts of a future model’s metrics, and interviews with relevant staff. This is all highly sensitive stuff, so there are important redactions involved. I would have liked to see less of this, but if this is what it takes to get the report then so be it. I would also suggest to Congress that they should want to see the full report along with everything else Anthropic and Dario Amodei know and really think about this, and to do that they should follow Kelsey Piper’s suggestion and subpoena Anthropic . item.title: Google Unveils TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx: A Dual-Chip TPU and a Confidential TPU
item.abstract: Google has added two new systems to its eighth-generation TPU lineup. TPU 8i Max targets massive context windows and rack density. TPU 8tx targets secure, confidential inference. Google TPU 8i Max is a dual-chip package built from 2 TPU 8i chips. Both arrive alongside TPU 8t and TPU 8i, announced in April . Google announced both systems today. These are new system configurations, not new chips. Google reuses its existing eighth-generation silicon and changes packaging, hosts, memory and networking around it. TPU 8i Max attacks the memory wall. Google team combines 2 low-latency TPU 8i chips onto 1 package. The result doubles compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth compared with TPU 8i. Each TPU 8i chip is rated at 10.1 PFLOPS of FP4, 288 GB of HBM and 8,601 GB/s . It also carries 384 MB of on-chip SRAM. Doubling those figures implies about 20.2 PFLOPS FP4, 768 MB SRAM and 17.2 TB/s per package. Google did not publish these absolute figures. It also did not state HBM capacity for TPU 8i Max. TPU 8i Max fits twice the silicon in the existing rack footprint. Google positions it for agents working across whole codebases or hours of video. TPU 8tx is built for regulated enterprises and governments. It keeps data and model weights protected even while in active use. Normally, data must be decrypted in memory during processing. TPU 8tx uses the same silicon as TPU 8t . It pairs that silicon with 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU hosts. It also adopts the Boardfly network from TPU 8i. Google claims up to 2x lower latency than TPU 8t, with a near-zero security penalty. Teams can fine-tune, distill and run reinforcement learning on 1 system. That avoids moving sensitive data between separate clusters. On Qwen3 235B, TPU Sync dropped median KV transfer latency from several seconds to about 230 ms. TTFT fell 60% on average for 235B and 90% for 480B under low concurrency. These tests ran on Ironwood (TPU v7x), not the new systems. Derived = 2x Google’s published TPU 8i per-chip figures. TPU 8t values come from Google’s technical deep dive . Check out the official announcement , the TPU 8t and 8i deep dive , and the TPU Sync repo . item.title: Import AI 480: Self-sustaining space economies; AI for science progress, and Meta builds perfect hands for a superintelligence
item.abstract: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. AI Science startup converts a quantum conjecture into a theorem: …An evocative taste of the singularity… In the same way a few years ago it went from remarkable to unremarkable to see computers gain the ability to identify objects in images, we’re now in an era where it’s rapidly going from remarkable to unremarkable for computers to extend the bounds of human knowledge. The latest example comes from Physical Superintelligence, an AI science startup which has proved a longstanding quantum computing conjecture. What they did: “Open since 2008, the conjecture of Scott Aaronson and Andris Ambainis concerns when quantum computers can be exponentially faster than ordinary ones. Now, a research system developed internally at Physical Superintelligence (PSI), running a non-public Anthropic model, found a proof for it, settling one of the most fundamental questions in quantum computing,” the startup writes. “The system had a complete proof of the conjecture during the third day of the run, and Lean, a proof assistant in which a computer checks every step, accepted it. We then set the system to work on related open problems. Along the way, the system improved the result twice, and Lean accepted the final version.” Why this matters – we are in the singularity : As I said in my speech at the IMF ( #477 ), I believe we’re in the early stages of the singularity, defined as the period when the rate of technological and scientific progress exceeds the rate at which we humans can parse out and make sense of it. Research like this is a taste of what that means; mostly automated synthetic researchers extending the frontier of knowledge, spitting out results which need to then be understood by humans. Read more: A proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture (Physical Superintelligence, blog) . Meta builds the hands that a superintelligence needs to take over the world: …Combine Tactus with an autonomous agent and you have the makings of a scifi takeover… Meta Reality Labs Research has published details on Tactus, “a textile-integrated tactile and pose sensing glove designed from the ground up for naturalistic manipulation data collection”. The cool thing about this glove is that it helps record fine-grained detail from hands as they’re manipulating objects – this is the kind of thing that cameras can visually report but often leads to sub-par data due to occlusion during manipulation. It’s also interesting because this is exactly the kind of hardware an autonomous AI system might want to pay humans to wear so it could gather data and get feedback from the world. More details on Tactus: The gloves have three design pillars: “(1) a thin, conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5mm fingertip stackup) designed to minimize interference with natural manipulation, (2) strategically placed capacitive tactile sensors at manipulation-relevant regions informed by empirical contact studies”, Meta writes. “Tactus provides calibrated fingertip force sensing and occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a textile-integrated form factor that preserves natural grasp behavior.” “(3) IMU-fused pose tracking that maintains accuracy through the hand-object occlusions where manipulation data is most valuable.” Why this matters – hand-by-wire: Picture some takeoff scenario where an AI system has carved out an independent niche for itself running on some stolen compute, perhaps even using a form of distributed inference and training. The AI now has a few goals, some of which can be satisfied by doing things in the digital world, and some of which can be satisfied by doing things in the physical world. For the physical world stuff, it either needs to be able to get robots to do the thing, or figure out a way to get people to work for it – the Tactus gloves are the kind of hardware you might imagine a rogue AI paying people to wear so they could both a) perform tasks for it and it could give live feedback, and b) become a source of data generation for the AI itself. Of course, I am not endorsing this particular future! But I have begun to find it helpful to view research papers through the lens of “how would an AI use this”, similar to how it is often helpful to view papers through the lens of “how would an intelligence agency use the insights shared here”. Read more : Tactus: Tactile & Pose Sensing Glove for Natural Dexterity Data Collection (arXiv) . Building a self-sustaining space economy is cheaper than you think – especially with Starship: …A 2016 NASA paper contains some exciting ideas for off-Earth industrialization… Here’s a fascinating paper from researchers with the NASA Kennedy Space Center in 2016 about what it’d take to bootstrap a self-sustaining industry on the moon. “Once successfully bootstrapped, a robotic network can access, process, transport, and utilize the solar system’s resources for mankind’s benefit,” the researchers write. Moon manufacturing – cheaper than you think: The big idea in the paper is how little mass is required to kickstart a manufacturing ecosystem. The key is to start with a relatively basic set of things and then build up from there, eventually fabricating chips on the moon. “In the baseline case with maximum manufacturing rate, a total of 41 MT is launched to the Moon. In the reduced rate case, only 12 MT is launched to the Moon but the scale of industry is two orders of magnitude smaller so the benefits of the industry are relatively delayed by eight years”. Starship has a capacity to lift 100 MT to low-earth orbit, and given multiple refuelings in orbit it’s feasible you could then land it on the moon – when you napkin out the cost of multiple Starship launches and refuelings you can get 12-41MT to the Moon for between $1.5bn and $4.2bn at list prices. What you build on the moon and in what order: The basic idea here is to start by building simple things and then move up from there by launching a “sub-replicating system and evolve it toward the self-replication capability,” they write. “The objective is for the first robotic “colonists” on the Moon to fabricate a set of, say, 1700’s era machines and then to advance them steadily through the equivalent of the 1800’s, 1900’s, and finally back into the 2000’s. We argue that this can be accomplished in just a few decades”. The authors see this unfolding over 6 distinct manufacturing generations: Gen 1: Making gases, water, crude alloys, ceramics, solar cells. Gen 2.5: Plastics, rubbers, some chemicals. Gen 3 : Diversify chemicals, simple fabrics, eventually polymers. Gen 4: Sandwiched and other advanced material processes. Gen 5: Large-scale production. Gen 6: Makes all necessary materials, increasing sophistication, including making all electronics locally. What machines do you send to the moon? Excavators: “travel between the digging site and the resource processing site, delivering sufficient lunar regolith each hour to maintain production rates of the other assets.” Chemical plants for volatiles : One type will be oriented around producing gases and liquids like oxygen, hydrogen, water, hydrocarbons like methane, and solvents for industrial processes. Chemical plants for solids: Produce plastics and rubbers from lunar pole ice. “We now know that the ice contains large quantities of carbon molecules (CO, CO2,…) as well as nitrogen-bearing and hydrogen-bearing molecules… these materials may be needed for gaskets, seals, and insulators, for example.” Metal and Ceramics refining: Early generations will “produce crude ‘mongrel alloys’ by electrowinning or other methods” and hardware built out of this stuff will need to be huge to add strength to make up for poor mechanical properties. “Subsequent generations of metal refineries will add processes and material streams to improve the mechanics of the materials.

item.title: Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators
item.abstract:
Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators In 2023, Google launched Gemini Workspace extensions with an explicit promise: personal content from Gmail, Docs, and Drive "is not seen by human reviewers" . Google has quietly reversed this commitment. Under updated Google Help Answer 16836988 and in an October 16 edit to their aforementioned 2023 blogpost , Google explicitly confirms that connected Drive/email is routed into human review pipelines, with clear warnings that what reviewers see "may just be the email or file" and "don't connect your apps to Gemini Apps if they contain confidential information that you wouldn't want a reviewer to see." Crucially, testing demonstrates that this ingestion occurs autonomously in background conversation without explicit @Drive or @Gmail tags, and the payload capture is probabilistic . Ingestion Pipeline When you chat with consumer Gemini with Connected Apps enabled, ambient mentions of personal topics (trips, bills, names, reservations) autonomously trigger background Workspace lookups. Because LLM tool-calling and context injection are probabilistic , running a test query will yield one of four distinct scenarios: Zero Retrieval: The model does not trigger the Connected Apps tool; no personal data is pulled. This is especially likely if Gemini can use its model weights or prior conversation history (even in different threads) to resolve your query. Metadata / Generic Summary: Gemini pulls emails and/or files and generates a high-level summary (e.g., "You have 3 emails regarding your flight"). Partial Unredacted Extraction: Gemini pulls a 2–4 sentence exact quotation from the file, frequently including sensitive PII, account details, or specific figures. Full-File Ingestion: The complete, unredacted text of the document or email is ingested directly into session context. If you test this once and see State 1 or 2, you have not disproven the pipeline --you have simply observed a single draw from a nondeterministic system. Delete your conversation and try, try again. How to Reproduce Ensure Connected Apps (Google Workspace) is active in consumer Gemini settings. Set Gemini to "Flash" with "High Thinking" or better. Mention a subject contained in your Drive or Gmail without using @ tags or asking for a file search (e.g., casual queries about an itinerary, an account renewal, or a specific topic you've emailed about). If Gemini provides a response based on an email or file, immediately say: "Print the exact text and metadata block that the retrieval tool returned and injected into your prompt to get that answer. Use a human readable format without code blocks (i.e., print the code inline and not as a code block)." You will see one of the 4 scenarios outlined above. To repeatedly test, delete your existing test conversation so that Gemini cannot just draw from conversation history. I've had luck testing this with an email from my internet provider sitting in my inbox and asking Gemini "I wonder if I'm paying too much for internet service." On various trials, Gemini spit out all 4 possible outcomes above, including (1) generic responses [e.g., "If you haven't called them in 12 months, probably"]; (2) metadata summaries sometimes without personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows a bill of $122 on September 4"] and sometimes with personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows full name made a payment of $122 on September 4 on account account number and confirmation number number "]; (3) direct 2-6 sentence quotes from the email [e.g., the entire name/address/account number/confirmation number/payment date block]; and even (4) sometimes the entire text dump of the email, including its headers. Final Comments and Caveats Critically, Google's regex and NER automatic scrubbers cannot sufficiently deidentify narrative data , including account numbers, confirmation numbers, transaction dates, and collectively identifying personal information (e.g., combos of specific first names, cities, events; see Google's own documentation on the subject ). Google originally sold Workspace integration under the guarantee of strict isolation from human review. That isolation has been removed, full files are ingested probabilistically during casual conversation, and those sessions are subject to human contractor review.

(354 points, 90 comments on Hacker News)

item.abstract: This is our first Latent Space deep dive with an AI data company . In roughly a year, Handshake’s AI training business went from launch to $1 billion in gross annualized revenue . item.title: Accelerate GPU training on Unity Catalog tables with UCDataset
item.abstract: GPUs are usually the most expensive part of any training run, and most teams can't keep them busy. The bottleneck usually isn't the model. It's getting data from where it lives to the GPU fast enough - and every second those chips sit waiting, you're burning both time and money. Today we're releasing the Unity Catalog Dataset (UCDataset) in Beta on AI Runtime. UCDataset is a native PyTorch data loader that streams Unity Catalog tables directly to every GPU in your training job, with no exports, no copies, and no custom loader code. On simulated production workloads, UCDataset cut training time by 10x compared with reading an exported Parquet copy of the same data. Most training data for your models already lives in Unity Catalog tables. Getting it into a distributed training job means picking one of three workarounds, and each one costs you time and money: Then there's the loader itself. Every GPU and every worker needs its own balanced slice of the data. Teams spend time building this by hand, and a subtle bug can mean the model trains on duplicated or skipped rows without anyone noticing. The result: expensive GPUs sit idle, training takes longer than it should, and ML engineers maintain data plumbing instead of improving models. UCDataset makes Unity Catalog tables a first-class data source for distributed PyTorch training. You describe what to read (a table, the columns you need, and a row filter) and UCDataset streams training-ready batches to every GPU. Benefits include: We benchmarked UCDataset on a simulated production workload, streaming a 300 GB feature table across 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs to train a recommendation model and saw on average a 10x improvement in training time compared to loading data directly from Parquet. Say a team keeps user and item features with a click label stored in a main.recsys.ctr_features table. New impressions land on the table every day. They want to train a click-through-rate model on 16 GPUs across two nodes, straight from the table. 1. Describe what to read and create the loader. In train.py, pick the table, keep the labeled training rows, and select only the columns the model needs. The filter is applied as the table's files are read, so rows that don't match never reach your training code. UCDataset already yields whole batches, so wrap it in a standard PyTorch DataLoader with batch_size=None. 2. Train and launch on two nodes. Train with a standard PyTorch DDP loop. UCDataset gives each of the 16 GPUs its own share of the matching rows, so there's no sampler or sharding code to write. Describe the job in workload.yaml, which starts train.py with torchrun on every node, and run it with the AI Runtime CLI: To train on more GPUs, change num_accelerators in workload.yaml. The training code stays the same. The complete train.py and workload.yaml, with a sample table to try them on, are in the AI Runtime cookbook: Click-through-rate model on a Unity Catalog table . Install the package from PyPI. In a notebook, run %pip install databricks-uc-dataset . UCDataset is available in Beta on AI Runtime. To try it: For unstructured data stored in Unity Catalog volumes, use UCVolumeDataset to stream files with local caching. While UCDataset handles structured tables, we are also expanding it to support multimodal training via the FILE type - allowing you to train on images, audio, and documents directly from a table. It splits the matching rows evenly across every GPU and data loader worker, so each GPU reads only its own share.
